Approximately 1,800 of the world's 10,000 bird species undertake long-distance migrations annually .
The timing of these movements is primarily controlled by changes in day length, which trigger hormonal changes within the birds' bodies .
**Navigation Cues:** **Celestial Navigation:** Diurnal migrants use a sun compass to navigate by day; they compensate for the changing position of the sun using an internal clock .
At night or during nocturnal migration, birds often rely on a stellar compass that depends on the position of constellations surrounding Polaris .
**Magnetoreception:** Many species possess the ability to sense the Earth's geomagnetic field through specialized photoreceptors, providing orientation backed up by celestial cues .
This magnetic sensing is part of a complex navigation system that may include both endogenous programs and learning .
In studies involving Cory’s shearwaters released 800 km from their home nests, birds rendered anosmic (unable to smell) took longer to return than control or magnetically disturbed birds .
Similarly, in experiments where birds were made anosmic with zinc sulphate, they failed to home before nightfall compared to controls .

**Visual Landmarks:** Navigation also involves the use of visual landmarks and mental maps formed by long-distance migrants who disperse as young birds and develop high site-fidelity to specific breeding and wintering locations .
For instance, rendering Procellariiformes anosmic delays their homing ability .
Additionally, magnetic disturbance has been tested alongside olfactory impairment; in one study, magnetically disturbed or control birds returned faster than anosmic ones when released 800 km away .
Historically, experiments have shown that interfering with astronomical cues (such as those used by procellariiforms) causes them to fly "as if lost" and return slowly or not at all .

**Evidence of Precision and Distance:** The precision of bird navigation is demonstrated by the Manx shearwater, which was released in Boston in a 1950 experiment and returned to its colony in Skomer, Wales within 13 days, covering a distance of 5,150 km (3,200 mi) .
While some birds like albatrosses circle the Earth, others such as Manx shearwaters migrate 14,000 km (8,700 mi) between northern breeding grounds and southern oceans .
The Arctic tern holds the record for the longest migration journey, traveling at least 19,000 km (12,000 mi) annually from the Arctic to the Antarctic and back .
